Write $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$ for the complex-valued smooth functions of compact support on the Euclidean plane. For $u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, $n=1$ or $2$, use the compact-support Riemann Fourier transform
$$\widehat u(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}u(x)e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\,dx.$$
For $\theta=(\theta_1,\theta_2)\in S^1:=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:|x|=1\}$ put $\theta^\perp=(-\theta_2,\theta_1)$. The line with normal $\theta$ and signed offset $s$ is $\{x\in\mathbb R^2:x\cdot\theta=s\}$. Its **Euclidean Radon transform** is
$$Rf(\theta,s):=\int_{\mathbb R}f(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)\,dt,\qquad f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C),\ (\theta,s)\in S^1\times\mathbb R.$$
The line integral is a compact-support Riemann integral.
The full data set uses every oriented normal $\theta\in S^1$ and every $s\in\mathbb R$; the same unoriented line is represented by $(\theta,s)$ and $(-\theta,-s)$.
For a one-dimensional function $h\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$, define
$$|D_s|h(s):=\int_{\mathbb R}2\pi|\sigma|\,\widehat h(\sigma)e^{2\pi i s\sigma}\,d\sigma.$$
For $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$ define the Riesz potential notation used here by
$$|D|^{-1}f(x):=\int_{\mathbb R^2}e^{2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\frac{\widehat f(\xi)}{2\pi|\xi|}\,d\xi.$$
The quotient in the last integral is assigned value $0$ at $\xi=0$. These integrals are absolutely convergent on the stated classes: compact-support integration by parts gives rapid decay of $\widehat f$ and $\widehat h$, while $\widehat f$ is bounded near $0$ and $|\xi|^{-1}$ is locally integrable in two dimensions. Here the multiplier for $|D_s|$ is $2\pi|\sigma|$, corresponding to the $e^{-2\pi i s\sigma}$ Fourier convention.
Every continuous real function on a compact Jordan measurable set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is Riemann integrable over $E$.

Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be nondegenerate closed rectangles, and let $f:A\times B\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Then the four lower and upper section-integral functions of [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]] are Riemann integrable and
$$\int_A\ell_B=\int_Au_B=\int_{A\times B}f=\int_B\ell_A=\int_Bu_A.$$

If the $B$-sections are integrable outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq A$, every bounded exceptionally completed function $h$ with $h(x)=\int_Bf_x$ for $x\notin N$ is integrable and
$$\int_{A\times B}f=\int_Ah.$$
The same assertion holds with the coordinate blocks exchanged. In particular, when every section in an order is integrable, the ordinary iterated integral in that order exists and equals the multiple integral. The theorem does not assert that every section of an integrable function is integrable.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $g:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be injective and $C^1$, with $Dg(x)$ invertible on $U$. Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be compactly supported Riemann integrable and suppose $\operatorname{supp}f\subseteq g(U)$. Define
$$h(x)=\begin{cases}f(g(x))|\det Dg(x)|,&x\in U,\\0,&x\notin U.\end{cases}$$
Then $h$ is compactly supported Riemann integrable and
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(y)\,dy=\int_{\mathbb R^n}h(x)\,dx.$$

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

derivations.claim: Fix $\theta$ and define $T(s,t)=s\theta+t\theta^\perp$ and $F(s,t)=f(T(s,t))$. The columns of $T$ are an orthonormal positively oriented basis, so $T$ is a linear diffeomorphism and $K:=T^{-1}(\operatorname{supp}f)$ is compact. Choose $M>0$ with $K\subset[-M,M]^2$. Then $F(s,t)=0$ for $|t|>M$, and $Rf(\theta,s)=\int_{-M}^{M}F(s,t)\,dt$; it vanishes unless $s$ belongs to the compact projection of $K$ onto the first coordinate.

Write $f=f_{\mathrm R}+if_{\mathrm I}$ and $F_
u=f_
u\circ T$ for $
u\in\{\mathrm R,\mathrm I\}$. Each $f_
u$ is real smooth; since $DT$ is constant, repeated applications of [F6] give $\partial_s^kF_
u(s,t)=(	heta\cdot
abla)^k f_
u(T(s,t))$. Thus, for each integer $k\ge0$, $\partial_s^kF$ is continuous. On every compact $s$-interval, $\partial_s^{k+1}F$ is uniformly continuous on the product with $[-M,M]$. For each real component, apply [F5] on $[0,1]$ to $u\mapsto\partial_s^kF_
u(s+uh,t)$. By [F6] its derivative is $h\,\partial_s^{k+1}F_
u(s+uh,t)$, continuous and hence integrable by [F2], with the same one-sided derivatives at the endpoints. Combining the two real equalities and dividing by $h$ gives, for sufficiently small nonzero $h$ of either sign, $$ rac{\partial_s^kF(s+h,t)-\partial_s^kF(s,t)}{h}=\int_0^1\partial_s^{k+1}F(s+uh,t)\,du.$$ The right side converges uniformly for $t\in[-M,M]$ to $\partial_s^{k+1}F(s,t)$ as $h	o0$. Integrating in $t$ therefore proves inductively that $ rac{d^k}{ds^k}Rf(	heta,s)=\int_{-M}^{M}\partial_s^kF(s,t)\,dt$ for every $k$, and uniform continuity also makes each derivative continuous in $s$. Thus $Rf(	heta,\cdot)\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$, so its Fourier transform in [F1] is defined.

Put $H(s,t)=f(T(s,t))e^{-2\pi i\sigma s}$. This is continuous and supported in $K$. Choose a nondegenerate product rectangle containing $K$. By [F2], the real and imaginary parts of $H$ are Riemann integrable there, and all their one-variable sections are continuous and hence Riemann integrable.

By [F1], $\widehat{Rf}(\theta,\sigma)$ is the iterated integral of $H$, first in $t$ and then in $s$. Apply the real-valued Riemann-Fubini theorem [F3] separately to $\operatorname{Re}H$ and $\operatorname{Im}H$ on the chosen rectangle, then combine the two equalities. Since $H$ vanishes outside that rectangle, this gives $$\widehat{Rf}(\theta,\sigma)=\int_{\mathbb R^2}f(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)e^{-2\pi i\sigma s}\,ds\,dt.$$

Apply [F4] to $T$ separately for the real and imaginary parts of the compactly supported Riemann integrand in step 3.1. Since $s=x\cdot\theta$ and $|\det DT|=1$, the integral becomes $\int_{\mathbb R^2}f(x)e^{-2\pi i\sigma x\cdot\theta}\,dx=\widehat f(\sigma\theta)$ by [F1]. This is the claimed identity.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Write $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$ for the complex-valued smooth functions of compact support on the Euclidean plane. For $u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, $n=1$ or $2$, use the compact-support Riemann Fourier transform
$$\widehat u(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}u(x)e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\,dx.$$
For $\theta=(\theta_1,\theta_2)\in S^1:=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:|x|=1\}$ put $\theta^\perp=(-\theta_2,\theta_1)$. The line with normal $\theta$ and signed offset $s$ is $\{x\in\mathbb R^2:x\cdot\theta=s\}$. Its **Euclidean Radon transform** is
$$Rf(\theta,s):=\int_{\mathbb R}f(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)\,dt,\qquad f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C),\ (\theta,s)\in S^1\times\mathbb R.$$
The line integral is a compact-support Riemann integral.
The full data set uses every oriented normal $\theta\in S^1$ and every $s\in\mathbb R$; the same unoriented line is represented by $(\theta,s)$ and $(-\theta,-s)$.
For a one-dimensional function $h\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$, define
$$|D_s|h(s):=\int_{\mathbb R}2\pi|\sigma|\,\widehat h(\sigma)e^{2\pi i s\sigma}\,d\sigma.$$
For $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$ define the Riesz potential notation used here by
$$|D|^{-1}f(x):=\int_{\mathbb R^2}e^{2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\frac{\widehat f(\xi)}{2\pi|\xi|}\,d\xi.$$
The quotient in the last integral is assigned value $0$ at $\xi=0$. These integrals are absolutely convergent on the stated classes: compact-support integration by parts gives rapid decay of $\widehat f$ and $\widehat h$, while $\widehat f$ is bounded near $0$ and $|\xi|^{-1}$ is locally integrable in two dimensions. Here the multiplier for $|D_s|$ is $2\pi|\sigma|$, corresponding to the $e^{-2\pi i s\sigma}$ Fourier convention.

For every $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$, every unit normal $\theta\in S^1$, and every $\sigma\in\mathbb R$, the compact-support Fourier transform of the line data in the offset variable equals the restriction of the two-dimensional Fourier transform to the line in frequency space with direction $\theta$:
$$\widehat{Rf}(\theta,\sigma)=\widehat f(\sigma\theta).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix $n \ge 1$
and write
$$S^{n-1}:=\{\omega \in \mathbb R^n : |\omega|=1\}.$$
Let
$$\Phi:\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}\longrightarrow(0,\infty)\times S^{n-1},\qquad \Phi(x)=(|x|,x/|x|).$$
This map is continuous. If $E\subseteq S^{n-1}$ is Borel, then
$(0,1]\times E$ is Borel and
$$\{r\omega:\omega\in E,\ 0<r\le1\}=\Phi^{-1}((0,1]\times E)$$
is Borel in $\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$ by
[[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]], hence Borel in
$\mathbb R^n$ by [[thm-borel-sigma-algebra-of-a-subspace-is-the-trace]]. It is
therefore Lebesgue measurable by [[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]].
Define
$$\sigma(E):=n\,\lambda_n(\{r\omega : \omega \in E,\ 0<r\le 1\}).$$

The next theorem proves that this is a Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ and that it
is exactly the surface measure needed for polar coordinates.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
(The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)) and let $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be linear
with matrix $A$ (Linear map between vector spaces over the same field,
Every Euclidean linear map has a unique matrix and satisfies $\|Lh\|_2\le K\|h\|_2$ for some $K\ge0$).

1. **Invertible case.** If $\det A \ne 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable for
   every Lebesgue measurable $E$ and
   $$\lambda_n\big(T[E]\big) \;=\; |\det A|\;\lambda_n(E),$$
   both sides possibly $+\infty$; the product is defined in
   $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ because $|\det A| > 0$.
2. **Singular case.** If $\det A = 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ for **every** $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$.

**The singular clause is stated as nullity and not as a product.** When
$\det A = 0$ and $\lambda_n(E) = +\infty$ the expression
$|\det A|\,\lambda_n(E)$ is $0\cdot(+\infty)$, which The extended real line $\overline{\mathbb{R}} = \mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty, +\infty\}$, its order, and the arithmetic that is left undefined
leaves undefined; writing the conclusion as $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ says the same
thing wherever the product is defined and remains a statement where it is not.

Assume countable choice. The negative-sign, $2\pi$-normalized Fourier transform is continuous $\mathcal F:\mathcal S\to\mathcal S$, and
$$\mathcal F(\partial^\alpha f)(\xi)=(2\pi i\xi)^\alpha\widehat f(\xi),\qquad \partial^\beta\widehat f=\mathcal F((-2\pi ix)^\beta f).$$

Assume countable choice. For every $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ and every $x\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$f(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,d\xi.$$
The integral is absolutely convergent.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $Q=\prod_{i=1}^n[a_i,b_i]$ with $n\ge1$ and $a_i<b_i$. If a bounded Borel real function $f$ on $Q$ is Riemann integrable, then it is Lebesgue integrable and the two integrals agree. The corresponding assertion for complex functions holds componentwise. In particular it applies to smooth compact test integrands and their bounded Borel zero extensions from compact Jordan regions.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$
Every continuous real function on a compact Jordan measurable set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is Riemann integrable over $E$.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n$ is sigma-finite ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]):
   the cubes $(-k,k]^n$ are Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n\big((-k,k]^n\big) = (2k)^n < +\infty$, they increase with $k$, and
   their union over $k \in \mathbb{N}$ is $\mathbb{R}^n$.

If $T$ preserves $\mu$ and $f:X\to[0,\infty]$ is measurable, then $\int f\circ T\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu$, allowing infinity. If $f$ is integrable real or complex valued, $f\circ T$ is integrable and the same equality holds. Conversely, for a measurable self-map, equality for every measurable indicator implies measure preservation.

derivations.claim:
Since $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)$, it is a Schwartz function. Choose $R>0$ with $\operatorname{supp}f\subset B_R(0)$. For every $	heta\in S^1$ and $s\in\mathbb R$, the integrand $f(s	heta+t	heta^\perp)$ vanishes for $|t|>R$, because $|s	heta+t	heta^\perp|^2=s^2+t^2$. Thus the line integral is over the fixed interval $[-R,R]$. On every bounded $s$-interval, $(	heta,s,t)\mapsto f(s	heta+t	heta^\perp)$ is uniformly continuous on the compact parameter product with $S^1$ and $[-R,R]$, so its integral is jointly continuous in $(	heta,s)$. For fixed $	heta$, write $f=f_{\mathrm R}+if_{\mathrm I}$ and $F_
u(s,t)=f_
u(s	heta+t	heta^\perp)$ for $
u\in\{\mathrm R,\mathrm I\}$. The inner coordinate map is linear with constant derivative, so repeated use of [F12] gives $\partial_s^kF_
u(s,t)=(	heta\cdot
abla)^k f_
u(s	heta+t	heta^\perp)$ for every $k$. Apply [F11] on $[0,1]$ to each real function $u\mapsto\partial_s^kF_
u(s+uh,t)$: by [F12] its derivative is $h\,\partial_s^{k+1}F_
u(s+uh,t)$, which is continuous and Riemann integrable by [F13], including at the endpoints. Dividing the resulting identity by any nonzero $h$ gives the difference quotient as the $u$-integral of $\partial_s^{k+1}F_
u(s+uh,t)$. Uniform continuity on each compact $(s,t)$ rectangle makes this converge uniformly in $t\in[-R,R]$; integrating and recombining the two real components therefore gives $\partial_s^k Rf(	heta,s)=\int_{-R}^{R}(	heta\cdot
abla)^k f(s	heta+t	heta^\perp)\,dt$ for every $k\ge0$, with each derivative continuous. Also $Rf(	heta,s)=0$ for $|s|>R$, so $Rf(	heta,\cdot)\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$ and is Schwartz. For every $x$, joint continuity makes $	heta\mapsto Rf(	heta,x\cdot	heta)$ continuous; [F4] makes $\mu$ finite, so the defining backprojection integral exists. By [F6] and [F7], the Lebesgue Fourier transforms of $f$ and $Rf(	heta,\cdot)$ are Schwartz and satisfy pointwise inversion; [F8] identifies them with the compact-support Riemann transforms in [F1]. Also $|\widehat f(\xi)|\le\int|f|$, and [F4] shows $|\xi|^{-1}\widehat f(\xi)$ is integrable near $0$; outside the unit disk it is dominated by the integrable Schwartz function $|\widehat f|$. Rapid decay of $\widehat f$ and finiteness of $\mu$ make the later signed-frequency integrals absolutely convergent.

Apply [F7] to $Rf(\theta,\cdot)$ at $s=x\cdot\theta$, then substitute the slice identity [F2] to get $Rf(\theta,x\cdot\theta)=\int_{\mathbb R}\widehat f(\sigma\theta)e^{2\pi i\sigma x\cdot\theta}\,d\sigma$. By [F4], $\mu$ is finite, and by [F14] Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R$ is sigma-finite, so the measure spaces in [F9] are sigma-finite. The integrand is continuous; since $\widehat f$ is Schwartz, $|\widehat f(\sigma\theta)|\le C_N(1+|\sigma|)^{-N}$ uniformly in $\theta$, and choosing $N>1$ shows it is absolutely integrable on their product. Thus [F9] permits either order of integration and gives $R^*Rf(x)=\int_{S^1}\int_{\mathbb R}\widehat f(\sigma\theta)e^{2\pi i\sigma x\cdot\theta}\,d\sigma\,d\mu(\theta)$.

The polar definition [F3] and change of variables [F5] imply $\mu(-E)=\mu(E)$ for every Borel $E\subseteq S^1$, since the cone of $-E$ is the image under $-I$ of the cone of $E$ and $|\det(-I)|=1$. Thus $\theta\mapsto-\theta$ preserves $\mu$. The reflection $\sigma\mapsto-\sigma$ preserves Lebesgue measure by [F5] in dimension one. Both maps are Borel, so [F15] permits these substitutions in the integrable angular and frequency integrands. Split the $\sigma$-integral in step 2.1 at zero and use $r=-\sigma$ and $\theta\mapsto-\theta$ on its negative half to obtain twice the positive-half integral. Apply [F4] to $h(\xi)=\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi i x\cdot\xi}/|\xi|$, set to zero at $\xi=0$; for complex $h$, apply the nonnegative formula to positive and negative real and imaginary parts and use [F10]. Thus $R^*Rf(x)=2\int_{\mathbb R^2}\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi i x\cdot\xi}|\xi|^{-1}d\lambda_2(\xi)=4\pi|D|^{-1}f(x)$.

By [F1] and [F2], $|D_s|Rf(\theta,s)=\int_{\mathbb R}2\pi|\sigma|\widehat f(\sigma\theta)e^{2\pi i s\sigma}\,d\sigma$. Schwartz decay gives a bound $|\widehat f(\sigma\theta)|\le C_N(1+|\sigma|)^{-N}$ uniform in $\theta$. On each compact parameter set $S^1\times[-A,A]$, the truncated integrals over bounded $\sigma$-intervals are continuous in $(\theta,s)$, while the displayed bound makes their tails uniformly tend to zero; hence the filtered data are jointly continuous. The same bound gives absolute convergence and boundedness, so finiteness of $\mu$ makes the backprojection integral exist. For fixed $x$, the product integrand $2\pi|\sigma|\widehat f(\sigma\theta)e^{2\pi i\sigma x\cdot\theta}$ is continuous and absolutely integrable by the same bound with $N>2$. The measure spaces are sigma-finite as established in step 2.1; Fubini [F9], the signed-frequency split in step 3.1, and [F4] give $R^*|D_s|Rf(x)=4\pi\int_{\mathbb R^2}\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi i x\cdot\xi}d\lambda_2(\xi)=4\pi f(x)$ by [F7].
Step 3.1 is the normal-operator identity, and dividing step 4.1 by $4\pi$ gives the filtered-backprojection identity. Both hold pointwise for every $x\in\mathbb R^2$.

boundaries.evidence: For f=0 both displayed identities have zero integrands in steps 2.1 and 4.1.
The inverse-symbol singularity at xi=0 is assigned value zero and is locally integrable by step 1.1.

boundaries.reason: The constant-one function is not compactly supported on R² and is outside the theorem's domain.

boundaries.evidence: The ramp multiplier vanishes at zero frequency and the Riesz singularity is integrable there, as shown in step 1.1 and used in step 4.1.

boundaries.reason: Offsets and frequencies range over all of R and have no finite endpoints.

boundaries.evidence: Countable Choice is explicitly assumed and identified in step 1.1; no full AC or DC premise is used.

boundaries.reason: The statement asserts identities rather than an equivalence.
The statement asserts identities rather than an equivalence.

It depends on $\theta$ only through the norm identity, so the sinogram is radial-data independent of orientation. The continuous compactly supported integrands are Riemann integrable by [F2].

Write $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$ for the complex-valued smooth functions of compact support on the Euclidean plane. For $u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, $n=1$ or $2$, use the compact-support Riemann Fourier transform
$$\widehat u(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}u(x)e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\,dx.$$
For $\theta=(\theta_1,\theta_2)\in S^1:=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:|x|=1\}$ put $\theta^\perp=(-\theta_2,\theta_1)$. The line with normal $\theta$ and signed offset $s$ is $\{x\in\mathbb R^2:x\cdot\theta=s\}$. Its **Euclidean Radon transform** is
$$Rf(\theta,s):=\int_{\mathbb R}f(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)\,dt,\qquad f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C),\ (\theta,s)\in S^1\times\mathbb R.$$
The line integral is a compact-support Riemann integral.
The full data set uses every oriented normal $\theta\in S^1$ and every $s\in\mathbb R$; the same unoriented line is represented by $(\theta,s)$ and $(-\theta,-s)$.
For a one-dimensional function $h\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$, define
$$|D_s|h(s):=\int_{\mathbb R}2\pi|\sigma|\,\widehat h(\sigma)e^{2\pi i s\sigma}\,d\sigma.$$
For $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$ define the Riesz potential notation used here by
$$|D|^{-1}f(x):=\int_{\mathbb R^2}e^{2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\frac{\widehat f(\xi)}{2\pi|\xi|}\,d\xi.$$
The quotient in the last integral is assigned value $0$ at $\xi=0$. These integrals are absolutely convergent on the stated classes: compact-support integration by parts gives rapid decay of $\widehat f$ and $\widehat h$, while $\widehat f$ is bounded near $0$ and $|\xi|^{-1}$ is locally integrable in two dimensions. Here the multiplier for $|D_s|$ is $2\pi|\sigma|$, corresponding to the $e^{-2\pi i s\sigma}$ Fourier convention.
Every continuous real function on a compact Jordan measurable set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is Riemann integrable over $E$.

Let $Q=\prod_{j<m}[a_j,b_j]$ be nondegenerate. For integrable
$f,g:Q\to\mathbb R$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$, the function
$\alpha f+\beta g$ is integrable and its integral is
$\alpha\int_Qf+\beta\int_Qg$. If $f\le g$, then
$\int_Qf\le\int_Qg$. Also $|f|$ is integrable and
$|\int_Qf|\le\int_Q|f|$. If $a_r<c<b_r$, cutting $Q$ at the coordinate
hyperplane $x_r=c$ gives two nondegenerate subrectangles; integrability on
$Q$ is equivalent to integrability on both restrictions, and their integral
values add to the integral over $Q$.

Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be nondegenerate closed rectangles, and let $f:A\times B\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Then the four lower and upper section-integral functions of [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]] are Riemann integrable and
$$\int_A\ell_B=\int_Au_B=\int_{A\times B}f=\int_B\ell_A=\int_Bu_A.$$

If the $B$-sections are integrable outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq A$, every bounded exceptionally completed function $h$ with $h(x)=\int_Bf_x$ for $x\notin N$ is integrable and
$$\int_{A\times B}f=\int_Ah.$$
The same assertion holds with the coordinate blocks exchanged. In particular, when every section in an order is integrable, the ordinary iterated integral in that order exists and equals the multiple integral. The theorem does not assert that every section of an integrable function is integrable.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $g:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be injective and $C^1$, with $Dg(x)$ invertible on $U$. Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be compactly supported Riemann integrable and suppose $\operatorname{supp}f\subseteq g(U)$. Define
$$h(x)=\begin{cases}f(g(x))|\det Dg(x)|,&x\in U,\\0,&x\notin U.\end{cases}$$
Then $h$ is compactly supported Riemann integrable and
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(y)\,dy=\int_{\mathbb R^n}h(x)\,dx.$$

derivations.claim: For $u>0$, repeated differentiation gives $\eta^{(k)}(u)=P_k(1/u)e^{-1/u}$ for a polynomial $P_k$. The exponential-series bound $e^v\ge v^{m+1}/(m+1)!$ for $v>0$ shows that each such expression and its difference quotient tend to $0$ as $u\downarrow0$; induction on $k$ proves that the zero extension is smooth. Hence $\psi$ is smooth, nonnegative, vanishes for $|x|\ge1$, and is positive near $x=0$.

By [F2], $\psi$ is Riemann integrable on a bounding rectangle; $0\le\psi\le1$ and its support lies in $[-1,1]^2$, so [F3] gives $J<\infty$. On $[-1/4,1/4]^2$ one has $1-|x|^2\ge7/8$, hence $\psi\ge e^{-8/7}$; monotonicity in [F3] gives $J\ge e^{-8/7}/4>0$. Thus $\phi$ is defined, radial, smooth, compactly supported, nonnegative, and has integral one. Applying [F5] to $x=\varepsilon y$ gives $\int_{\mathbb R^2}\phi_\varepsilon(x)\,dx=\varepsilon^{-2}\varepsilon^2\int_{\mathbb R^2}\phi(y)\,dy=1$ for every $\varepsilon>0$.

The scaling $t=\varepsilon u$ in the line integral [F1] gives $R\phi_\varepsilon(\theta,s)=\varepsilon^{-1}\rho(s/\varepsilon)$. Radiality gives $\phi(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)=\phi(\sqrt{s^2+t^2})$, so $\rho$ is independent of $\theta$ and vanishes for $|s|>1$. It is continuous: for $s'\to s$, $$|\rho(s')-\rho(s)|\le2\sup_{|t|\le1}|\phi(s'\theta+t\theta^\perp)-\phi(s\theta+t\theta^\perp)|\longrightarrow0,$$ since $\phi$ is uniformly continuous. Thus $\rho$ is compactly supported and Riemann integrable by [F2]. Riemann-Fubini [F4] and the orthogonal change of variables $(s,t)\mapsto s\theta+t\theta^\perp$, whose absolute Jacobian is $1$, give $\int_{\mathbb R}\rho(s)\,ds=\int_{\mathbb R^2}\phi(x)\,dx=1$.

By step 3.1, $\rho$ is continuous and supported on $[-1,1]$, so $R\phi_\varepsilon(\theta,\cdot)h$ is compactly supported and continuous. If $h$ is complex-valued, apply [F2] and the compact-support change of variables [F5] separately to its real and imaginary parts; thus with $s=\varepsilon u$ we get $\int_{\mathbb R}R\phi_\varepsilon(\theta,s)h(s)\,ds=\int_{-1}^{1}\rho(u)h(\varepsilon u)\,du$. Uniform continuity of $h$ on $[-1,1]$ implies $\sup_{|u|\le1}|h(\varepsilon u)-h(0)|\to0$. Since $\rho\ge0$ and $\int\rho=1$ by step 3.1, the integral tends to $h(0)$.
The functional $h\mapsto h(0)$ is the point mass $\delta_0$ by definition of the Dirac distribution. Step 4.1 proves the asserted distributional limit for every fixed normal $\theta$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice and let $\mu$ be the polar surface measure on $S^1$, with $\mu(E)=2\lambda_2(\{r\theta:\theta\in E,\ 0<r\le1\})$ for Borel $E\subseteq S^1$. The **complete-data filtered-backprojection procedure** takes as input the exact full sinogram $g=Rf$ of some $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$; all oriented normals $\theta\in S^1$ and all offsets $s\in\mathbb R$ are supplied. It returns the function $f_{\mathrm{FBP}}:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb C$ defined by
$$f_{\mathrm{FBP}}(x)=\frac1{4\pi}\int_{S^1}q(\theta,x\cdot\theta)\,d\mu(\theta),$$
where the filter output is
$$q(\theta,s)=\int_{\mathbb R}2\pi|\sigma|\,\widehat{g(\theta,\cdot)}(\sigma)e^{2\pi i s\sigma}\,d\sigma.$$
The exact instructions are: (1) for each $\theta$, take the one-dimensional Fourier transform of $g(\theta,\cdot)$ with the negative-sign $2\pi$ convention; (2) multiply that transform by the declared ramp filter $2\pi|\sigma|$ and take its inverse Fourier integral to form $q(\theta,\cdot)$; (3) evaluate $q(\theta,\cdot)$ at $s=x\cdot\theta$ and integrate over the full polar surface measure in $\theta$; (4) divide by $4\pi$. For this input class the slice identity and Schwartz decay make the filter integral absolutely convergent and the backprojection integral well defined. This definition specifies the continuous full-data procedure; it gives no guarantee for finitely sampled, truncated, or noisy measurements. Exact recovery on the stated class is proved by the normal-operator theorem.

Let $m\in\mathbb N$ and $N=2^{m}$. The **radix-two fast Fourier transform** $\operatorname{FFT}_m:\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}\to\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$ is defined by recursion on $m$ as follows. At $m=0$ the group is $\mathbb Z/1\mathbb Z$ and $\operatorname{FFT}_0:=\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/1}}$. For $m\ge1$, given $f\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/2^{m}}$ with even and odd parts $e,o\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/2^{m-1}}$ ([[lem-radix-two-even-odd-dft-factorisation]]), and given $E:=\operatorname{FFT}_{m-1}(e)$ and $O:=\operatorname{FFT}_{m-1}(o)$, extend $E$ and $O$ from $\mathbb Z/2^{m-1}\mathbb Z$ to $\mathbb Z$ by $2^{m-1}$-periodicity and set

$$\operatorname{FFT}_m(f)(k):=E(k)+e^{-2\pi ik/2^{m}}O(k),\qquad k\in\mathbb Z.$$

Then $\operatorname{FFT}_m(f)(k+2^{m})=\operatorname{FFT}_m(f)(k)$ for every $k\in\mathbb Z$, because $E$ and $O$ are $2^{m-1}$-periodic and $e^{-2\pi i(k+2^{m})/2^{m}}=e^{-2\pi ik/2^{m}}e^{-2\pi i}=e^{-2\pi ik/2^{m}}$ ([[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-kernel-and-fibres-of-complex-exponential]]); hence $\operatorname{FFT}_m(f)$ factors through $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/2^{m}\mathbb Z$ and $\operatorname{FFT}_m$ is a well-defined map $\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/2^{m}}\to\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/2^{m}}$.

**The recursion is legitimate.** Put $\mathcal F_m:=\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/2^m}$ for each $m\in\mathbb N$, and use the tagged state set $A:=\{(m,g):m\in\mathbb N,\ g:\mathcal F_m\to\mathcal F_m\}$. For a state $(m,g)\in A$ and $f\in\mathcal F_{m+1}$, let $e,o\in\mathcal F_m$ be the even and odd parts supplied by [[lem-radix-two-even-odd-dft-factorisation]], and define $g^+(f)\in\mathcal F_{m+1}$ by $g^+(f)([k]_{2^{m+1}}):=g(e)([k]_{2^m})+e^{-2\pi ik/2^{m+1}}g(o)([k]_{2^m})$ for $k\in\mathbb Z$. This is well defined on $[k]_{2^{m+1}}$: replacing $k$ by $k+2^{m+1}$ leaves the recursive values unchanged modulo $2^m$ and multiplies the twiddle by $e^{-2\pi i}=1$ ([[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-kernel-and-fibres-of-complex-exponential]]). Thus $g^+$ is a total map $\mathcal F_{m+1}\to\mathcal F_{m+1}$, and $T:A\to A$ defined by $T(m,g):=(m+1,g^+)$ is a total step function. Starting from $a:=(0,\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal F_0})$, the recursion theorem [[thm-recursion]] gives a unique $H:\mathbb N\to A$ with $H(0)=a$ and $H(m+1)=T(H(m))$. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]], [[def-natural-numbers]]) the first coordinate of $H(m)$ is $m$; writing $H(m)=(m,\operatorname{FFT}_m)$ gives $\operatorname{FFT}_m:\mathcal F_m\to\mathcal F_m$ and exactly the base and combine clauses above. Termination is immediate from recursion on $m$: each recursive call uses level $m-1$, and the base case $m=0$ returns the input. The exponent arithmetic uses $2^{m+1}=2\cdot2^m$ and, for the rescaling below, $2^{-m/2}=(2^m)^{-1/2}$ ([[lem-power-laws]], [[def-rational-power]], [[lem-rational-power-laws]]).

**What the algorithm computes.** Correctness is proved separately later on this page: $\operatorname{FFT}_m(f)(k)=X_k(f)$ for every input, where $X$ is the unnormalised transform of [[def-unnormalised-engineering-dft-and-conversion]]; the unitary transform of this page is recovered from the output by the single rescaling $2^{-m/2}$ at length $N=2^{m}$. The operation count is likewise the subject of a later item. At level $m$ the recursion forms the even and odd parts of a length-$2^{m}$ list and performs one combine per output value, reading $E$ and $O$ at their classes and multiplying by the twiddle factors $e^{-2\pi ik/2^{m}}$.

Let $m\in\mathbb N$, $N=2^{m}$ and $f\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$. Then

$$\operatorname{FFT}_m(f)(k)=X_k(f)\qquad\text{for every }k\in\mathbb Z,$$

where $X$ is the unnormalised $N$-point discrete Fourier transform of [[def-unnormalised-engineering-dft-and-conversion]]. Equivalently $\operatorname{FFT}_m(f)=2^{m/2}\,\mathcal F_Nf$ for the unitary transform of [[def-unitary-discrete-fourier-transform-on-z-mod-n]]; consequently the algorithm returns the unitary transform after the single rescaling $2^{-m/2}$, and it does so for every input of length $2^{m}$. Correctness is separate from speed: the operation count is the subject of a different theorem, and no floating-point or stability claim is made here.

Let $N\ge1$ and $f\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$. The **unnormalised (engineering) discrete Fourier transform** of $f$ is the function $X(f):\mathbb Z\to\mathbb C$ defined by

$$X_k(f):=\sum_{x=0}^{N-1}f([x]_N)\,e^{-2\pi ikx/N},\qquad k\in\mathbb Z,$$

the sum being the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]] over the representatives $[0]_N,\dots,[N-1]_N$ of the classes of $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ ([[def-integers-modulo-n]]), with $e^z$ the complex exponential of [[def-complex-exponential]]. Comparing with [[def-unitary-discrete-fourier-transform-on-z-mod-n]],

$$X_k(f)=\sqrt N\,(\mathcal F_Nf)(k),\qquad (\mathcal F_Nf)(k)=N^{-1/2}X_k(f),\qquad k\in\mathbb Z,$$

where $\sqrt N=N^{1/2}$ is the rational power of [[def-rational-power]] and the two conversions are inverse to each other by $N^{1/2}N^{-1/2}=1$ ([[lem-rational-power-laws]]). So the two transforms determine each other, and the only difference between them is the constant $\sqrt N$.

**The transform is defined on classes and is $N$-periodic.** If $[x]_N=[x']_N$ then $x'=x+mN$ for some integer $m$ and $e^{-2\pi ikx'/N}=e^{-2\pi ikx/N}e^{-2\pi ikm}=e^{-2\pi ikx/N}$, so the summands depend only on classes; and $e^{-2\pi i(k+N)x/N}=e^{-2\pi ikx/N}e^{-2\pi ix}=e^{-2\pi ikx/N}$ for every integer $x$, both identities following from the addition law and $\exp(2\pi i\,\cdot)=1$ ([[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-kernel-and-fibres-of-complex-exponential]]). Hence $X(f)$ factors through $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$ and $X_k(f)$ depends on $k$ only through its class.

**Inverse formulas.** The inversion theorem in its unitary form is the identity $f(x)=N^{-1/2}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}(\mathcal F_Nf)(k)e^{2\pi ikx/N}$ of [[thm-finite-fourier-inversion]]; substituting $(\mathcal F_Nf)(k)=N^{-1/2}X_k(f)$ and collecting $N^{-1/2}N^{-1/2}=N^{-1}$ ([[lem-rational-power-laws]]) gives the engineering form

$$f(x)=\frac1N\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}X_k(f)\,e^{2\pi ikx/N},\qquad x\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z.$$

This is the convention in which the radix-two algorithm computes its output. The unitary transform is recovered by the single rescaling $N^{-1/2}=2^{-m/2}$ at length $N=2^m$. The correctness and complexity theorems refer to this unnormalised output; the convolution lemma is stated in the unitary convention.

Let $N\ge1$ and $f\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N}$. Then for every $x\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$

$$f(x)=N^{-1/2}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}(\mathcal F_Nf)(k)\,e^{2\pi ikx/N},$$

the right-hand side being independent of the chosen integer representative of the class $x$. Consequently $\mathcal F_N$ is bijective with inverse the positive-sign transform

$$(\mathcal G_Ng)(x):=N^{-1/2}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}g(k)\,e^{2\pi ikx/N},\qquad g\in\mathbb C^{\mathbb Z/N},\ x\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z,$$

and there is no convergence, regularity or support hypothesis anywhere.

The sampled ramp is $\lambda=(0,\pi/2,\pi,\pi/2)$, hence its filtered frequency array is $Y=(0,-\pi/2,\pi,-\pi/2)$.
The inverse formula [F4] gives $Q_m=\frac14\sum_{k=0}^3Y_ke^{2\pi i km/4}$. For $m=0,1,2,3$ the sums are respectively $0,-\pi,2\pi,-\pi$, so $Q=(0,-\pi/4,\pi/2,-\pi/4)$.
